analysis.one_liner: Lets people stop companies from collecting, selling, or sharing their personal data, and request deletion.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2019 with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies with more than $25 million in revenue (or that handle data on 50,000+ people, or make at least half their money selling data) to give people a chance to opt out before their personal information is collected, sold, or transferred. It would also let people demand that their data be deleted. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce these rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, whose names, addresses, phone numbers, email, Social Security numbers, account numbers, biometric data, and precise location would become things they can refuse to have collected and have deleted. Consumers could also benefit from state attorneys general suing violators for damages and restitution on their behalf.

how_it_helps.text: Covered entities must, before collecting covered data, give the individual an opportunity to prohibit collection or any sale or transfer of that data to a third party.
Upon request, a covered entity must delete the individual's covered data without undue delay, so people can have stored information removed.

Covered data includes personally identifiable information like names, addresses, email and phone numbers, Social Security numbers, credit card account numbers, biometric data such as fingerprints and retina scans, precise GPS-level location, and browsing-related identifiers.
The rules apply broadly to for-profit corporations, common carriers like phone and internet companies, and nonprofits, closing gaps that normally exempt nonprofits and carriers from FTC oversight.

The Federal Trade Commission can enforce the rules as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents to stop violations, force compliance, and obtain damages, restitution, or other compensation.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that live on personal data — data brokers, ad-supported platforms, telecom carriers, and any company above the size thresholds — would bear compliance costs and could lose revenue from selling or exploiting consumer data. That cost could be passed to consumers in some form, and businesses near the thresholds face new obligations regardless of data practices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad platforms, and large companies

drawbacks.text: The bill covers any entity with more than $25 million in gross annual revenue, plus nonprofits and common carriers, so even businesses with modest data footprints would face opt-out and deletion obligations.
Enforcement rests entirely with the FTC and state attorneys general; there is no private right of action, so individuals could not sue on their own behalf.

Data obtained from public records, public media, or forums where the person voluntarily and publicly shared it is exempt, and third parties defined as service providers are carved out, so some data flows would continue despite an opt-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is direct control over one of the most invasive practices of the modern economy: the quiet collection and sale of personal information. The costs are real but conventional — compliance burdens for businesses, some enforcement gaps because individuals cannot sue, and exemptions for publicly available data. On balance, the bill gives ordinary people a meaningful right they currently lack, at a cost borne mainly by the data industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, with no cosponsors, hearing, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on July 18, 2019.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction, the only Senate action it ever received.
The bill never advanced past committee before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so it never received a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, advertising-supported platforms, and other companies that profit from collecting and selling personal information — the bill that would have restricted them died in committee without a hearing, so their practices continued unchanged. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death; they simply kept the status quo they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that profit from personal data

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no other senator joined.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no markup, no hearing, no report — after it was referred on the day of introduction.

against.name: Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration of the bill during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic senator sponsored the bill and no Republican or other Democrat cosponsored it; the Republican-led Commerce Committee gave it no consideration.

industries.note: Companies that derive revenue from selling personal information would lose their raw material, since consumers could block collection and demand deletion. The bill even sets a specific trigger for firms getting 50% of revenue from data sales.

industries.industry: Ad-supported tech platforms and ad-tech firms
industries.note: Their business model depends on tracking individuals across sites and apps; an opt-out plus deletion rights would shrink the profiles they can build and monetize.

The bill explicitly brings common carriers under FTC-style enforcement for data practices, ending their usual exemption; they would face the same opt-out and deletion duties while losing a data advantage.

industries.industry: Large retailers and consumer-facing businesses generally
industries.note: Any entity over $25 million in revenue handling data on 50,000+ people would bear compliance costs for opt-out notices and deletion requests, though most are not primarily in the data business.
Nonprofits are expressly covered despite normally escaping FTC jurisdiction, so large nonprofits would face the same duties; many nonprofits, however, share their supporters' interest in privacy.
